## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]).

**Integral form.** Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be continuous. For a measurable $V\subseteq U$ write, componentwise,

$$\int_V g\,d\lambda_n:=\Bigl(\int g_1\chi_V\,d\lambda_n,\ \dots,\ \int g_m\chi_V\,d\lambda_n\Bigr),$$

each component, when integrable, being the Lebesgue integral of $g_i$ on $V$, extended by zero outside $V$ ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). A ball $V\subseteq U$ is **compactly contained** in $U$ when its closure is a compact subset of $U$; for a Euclidean ball this means $\overline V\subseteq U$. If $\int_Vg\,d\lambda_n=0$ for every ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$, then $g=0$ on $U$.

**Disc form.** Let $W\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:W\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Write $e_1=(1,0,0)$, $e_2=(0,1,0)$, $e_3=(0,0,1)$. For $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, $q\in W$ and $r>0$ put $e_{i+1}:=e_{(i\bmod 3)+1}$ cyclically, i.e. $e_{i+1}\times e_{i+2}=e_i$ in the cyclic order, and

$$\varphi_{i,q}(s,t):=q+s\,e_{i+1}+t\,e_{i+2},\qquad D_r:=\{(s,t)\in\mathbb R^2:s^2+t^2<r^2\},$$

with $\overline{D_r}$ the closed disc. If for every $i$, every $q\in W$ and every $r>0$ with $\varphi_{i,q}(\overline{D_r})\subseteq W$ one has

$$\int_{\overline{D_r}}(F_i\circ\varphi_{i,q})\,d\lambda_2=0,$$

then $F=0$ on $W$.

**Conventions.** The displayed disc condition is the vanishing of the flux of $F$ through the flat disc $\varphi_{i,q}(\overline{D_r})$ in the orientation with unit normal $e_i$: the affine parametrization is a regular patch whose tangent vectors $e_{i+1},e_{i+2}$ have cross product $e_i$ of norm one ([[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), so the flux of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]] is the Riemann integral $\int_{\overline{D_r}}(F_i\circ\varphi_{i,q})\,d(s,t)$; that integral equals the displayed Lebesgue integral because the integrand is continuous on the compact Jordan region $\overline{D_r}$ ([[cor-disc-jordan-content-is-pi-r-squared]], [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]], [[lem-bounded-borel-riemann-integrands-on-boxes-have-equal-lebesgue-integrals]]). Both clauses are pointwise conclusions on their open domains. The first clause is the converse from universal integral relations to a pointwise equation; a single vanishing integral over one ball or one disc supplies no conclusion, and the hypothesis ranges over the full family described.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The Axiom of Countable Choice; integers $n,m\ge1$; an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and a continuous $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ with $\int_Vg\,d\lambda_n=0$ for every ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$; an open $W\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and a continuous $F:W\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfying the disc condition of the Statement; and, inside the contradiction argument below, either a point $p\in U$ with $g(p)\ne0$ or a point $x\in W$ with $F(x)\ne0$.

[F1] Metric balls and continuity at a point: $B_X(a,\rho)=\{y\in X:d_X(y,a)<\rho\}$, and $f$ is continuous at $a$ when for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with $f[B_X(a,\delta)]\subseteq B_Y(f(a),\varepsilon)$ ([[def-metric-ball]], [[def-metric-continuity]]).

[F2] Open subsets of a metric space: $U$ is open exactly when every $x\in U$ has $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-topology]]).

[F3] Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, every Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty$ ([[lem-euclidean-balls-have-positive-finite-lebesgue-measure]]).

[F4] Integral of signed and nonnegative functions: for measurable real $u$ with at most one of $\int u^+$, $\int u^-$ equal to $+\infty$ one sets $\int u\,d\lambda:=\int u^+d\lambda-\int u^-d\lambda$, and $u$ is integrable when both are finite, equivalently $\int|u|\,d\lambda<\infty$; then $\int(-u)\,d\lambda=-\int u\,d\lambda$; and for nonnegative measurable $f$ the integral over $E$ is $\int_Ef\,d\lambda=\int f\chi_E\,d\lambda$ ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]).

[F5] Monotonicity and nonnegative homogeneity for the nonnegative integral: if $0\le f\le h$ are measurable then $\int f\,d\lambda\le\int h\,d\lambda$, and if $c>0$ then $\int cf\,d\lambda=c\int f\,d\lambda$ ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]).

[F6] Simple integral: for a nonnegative simple measurable function $s=\sum_{j\le N}c_j\chi_{E_j}$ one has $\int s\,d\lambda=\sum_{j\le N}c_j\lambda(E_j)$ with $0\cdot\infty=0$, and the nonnegative integral of a nonnegative simple measurable function equals its simple integral; hence $\int c\chi_E\,d\lambda=c\lambda(E)$ for $c\ge0$ and measurable $E$ ([[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]).

[F7] Measurability: every continuous map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is Borel measurable under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; the Borel $\sigma$-algebra is generated by the open sets, so indicators of open sets are Borel ([[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

[F8] Closed bounded Euclidean sets are compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]). Extreme values: a continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space is bounded above and below and attains a maximum and a minimum ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** contradiction; assume the Statement fails, and contradict in turn a nonzero value of $g$ (cases (A)) and, under the disc hypothesis, a nonzero value of $F$ (case (B)).

1.1 Suppose the Statement fails. Then either (A) $g(p)\ne0$ for some $p\in U$, or (B) the disc condition holds and $F(x)\ne0$ for some $x\in W$; if neither holds then $g=0$ on $U$ and, whenever the disc condition holds, $F=0$ on $W$, which is exactly the Statement. We contradict (A) and (B) in turn. [given, assume-contra]

2.1 In case (A): choose a component index $i\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ with $g_i(p)\ne0$ and put $u:=g_i$. Replacing the $i$-th component of $g$ by its negative preserves the hypothesis, since $\int_V(-g_i)\,d\lambda=-\int_Vg_i\,d\lambda$ by [F4], and does not change whether $g$ vanishes; hence we may suppose $u(p)=2c$ with $c:=u(p)/2>0$. By [F1] applied to the continuous $u$ at $p$ with $\varepsilon=c$ there is $\delta_0>0$ with $|u(y)-u(p)|<c$ for all $y\in B(p,\delta_0)$; by [F2] and $p\in U$ there is $\delta_2>0$ with $B(p,\delta_2)\subseteq U$; put $\delta:=\min\{\delta_0,\delta_2\}>0$. Then the ball $V:=B(p,\delta/2)$ satisfies $\overline V\subseteq B(p,\delta)\subseteq U$, so $V$ is compactly contained in $U$, and $u(y)>u(p)-c=c$ for every $y\in V$. The hypothesis gives $\int_Vg\,d\lambda_n=0$, whose $i$-th component is $\int u\chi_V\,d\lambda=0$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F4, given, algebra]

2.2 In case (B): choose $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ with $F_i(x)\ne0$ and put $\varphi:=\varphi_{i,x}$, $W':=\varphi^{-1}[W]=\{(s,t):\varphi(s,t)\in W\}$ and $h:=F_i\circ\varphi:W'\to\mathbb R$, so that $h(0,0)=F_i(x)\ne0$. Then $W'$ is open in $\mathbb R^2$, $h$ is continuous, and for every $r>0$ with $\overline B((0,0),r)\subseteq W'$ the disc hypothesis with centre $x$ gives $\int_{\overline B((0,0),r)}h\,d\lambda_2=0$. Indeed, the standard unit vectors are orthonormal ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), so $\lVert\varphi(s,t)-\varphi(s',t')\rVert_2=\lVert(s,t)-(s',t')\rVert_2$ for all $(s,t),(s',t')$; hence $\varphi$ is continuous and $W'$ is open by [F2], while for $(s_0,t_0)\in W'$ and $\varepsilon>0$, continuity of $F_i$ at $\varphi(s_0,t_0)\in W$ gives $\rho>0$ with $|F_i(y)-F_i(\varphi(s_0,t_0))|<\varepsilon$ whenever $d(y,\varphi(s_0,t_0))<\rho$, and then $d((s,t),(s_0,t_0))<\rho$ gives $|h(s,t)-h(s_0,t_0)|<\varepsilon$ by the isometry identity; finally, when $\overline B((0,0),r)\subseteq W'$ the disc $\varphi(\overline B((0,0),r))$ lies in $W$, so the Statement's condition applies with centre $x$ and radius $r$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

3.1 In case (A): the function $u\chi_V$ is Borel and nonnegative, and $0\le c\chi_V\le u\chi_V$ pointwise, because $u>c>0$ on $V$ by step 2.1 while $u\chi_V=0$ off $V$, and $u$ is continuous while $V$ is open [F7]. More explicitly, for a continuous function on open $U$, inverse images of open real sets are relatively open, hence open in $\mathbb R^n$; after multiplication by $\chi_V$ and zero extension, inverse images are Borel (adding $\mathbb R^n\setminus V$ when the target contains zero). Moreover $\overline V$ is a nonempty compact metric space, so $M:=\max_{\overline V}|u|$ is finite by [F8], and $|u\chi_V|\le M\chi_{B(p,\delta)}$ with $\int M\chi_{B(p,\delta)}\,d\lambda=M\lambda(B(p,\delta))<\infty$ by [F5], [F6] and [F3]; hence $u\chi_V$ is integrable and $\int u\chi_V\,d\lambda$ is a finite real number by [F4]. Monotonicity [F5] and the simple-integral rule [F6] give $\int u\chi_V\,d\lambda\ge\int c\chi_V\,d\lambda=c\,\lambda(V)>0$ by [F3], contradicting $\int u\chi_V\,d\lambda=0$ from step 2.1. Therefore case (A) is impossible: the integral hypothesis forces $g=0$ on $U$. [step 2.1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

4.1 In case (B), replace $h$ by $-h$ if necessary, which preserves every zero disc integral by [F4], so $h(0,0)=2c'>0$. Continuity and openness as in step 2.1 give $r>0$ with $\overline B((0,0),r)\subseteq W'$ and $h>c'$ throughout that closed disc $C$. It is compact by [F8] and contained in the open ball $B((0,0),2r)$, of finite measure by [F3], so $h\chi_C$ is integrable by the boundedness and Borel argument of step 3.1. Since $0\le c'\chi_{B((0,0),r)}\le h\chi_C$, [F5] and [F6] give $\int_C h\,d\lambda_2\ge c'\lambda_2(B((0,0),r))>0$ by [F3]. This contradicts the closed-disc integral hypothesis of step 2.2, without replacing it by an unstated open-ball hypothesis. Thus $F=0$ on $W$. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F8, algebra]

5.1 Cases (A) and (B) both end in contradiction, so no failure of the Statement occurs: the integral hypothesis forces $g=0$ on $U$, and the disc hypothesis forces $F=0$ on $W$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, discharge-contradiction] ∎

## Remarks

- The proof uses, for each clause, the hypothesis only on balls centred at the point where the function is assumed nonzero and with radius half of a continuity threshold; the full family in the Statement is what makes the lemma a localization statement, but no choice from the family is made, and the argument is choice-free apart from the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ used by the surface and measurability suppliers.
- The disc clause is not a statement about a single loop or box: one special disc carries no information, and the components must be tested in all three coordinate directions at all admissible centres and radii.

after.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $F^{n}$ be the
function space on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, with the
pointwise operations ([[def-function-space]], [[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). For $i < n$ define the **standard unit vector**
$e_i \in F^{n}$ by

$$e_i(i) = 1_F, \qquad e_i(j) = 0_F \ \text{ for } j < n \text{ with } j \ne i .$$

Then:

1. **Finite sums in a function space are pointwise.** For every set $X$, every
   $p \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $u : p \to F^{X}$ and every $j \in X$,
   $$\Bigl(\sum_{k<p} u_k\Bigr)(j) \;=\; \sum_{k<p} u_k(j),$$
   the right-hand sum being taken in $(F,+,0_F)$. (Stated here for an arbitrary
   $X$ because the companion page needs it at $X = \mathbb{N}$.)
2. $e : n \to F^{n}$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$ ([[def-linear-basis]]); in
   particular $e$ is injective and its image $e[n] = \{\, e_i : i < n \,\}$ is a
   basis of $F^{n}$ with $e[n] \approx n$ ([[def-equinumerous]]);
3. for every $\lambda : n \to F$ and every $j < n$,
   $\bigl(\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i e_i\bigr)(j) = \lambda_j$; equivalently the
   coordinate list of $x \in F^{n}$ with respect to the ordered basis $e$
   ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) is
   $i \mapsto x(i)$;
4. $F^{n}$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ with $\dim_F F^{n} = n$
   ([[def-dimension]]);
5. at $n = 0$ this reads: $F^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
   so $F^{0}$ is the zero space, the empty list is its ordered basis,
   $\varnothing$ is its basis and $\dim_F F^{0} = 0$.

Every index runs from $0$, so the coordinates of an element of $F^{n}$ are
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and no statement above is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]).

**Integral form.** Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be continuous. For a measurable $V\subseteq U$ write, componentwise,

$$\int_V g\,d\lambda_n:=\Bigl(\int g_1\chi_V\,d\lambda_n,\ \dots,\ \int g_m\chi_V\,d\lambda_n\Bigr),$$

each component, when integrable, being the Lebesgue integral of $g_i$ on $V$, extended by zero outside $V$ ([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). A ball $V\subseteq U$ is **compactly contained** in $U$ when its closure is a compact subset of $U$; for a Euclidean ball this means $\overline V\subseteq U$. If $\int_Vg\,d\lambda_n=0$ for every ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$, then $g=0$ on $U$.
